narrative:
The model estimated about a 49% chance that you will leave, which is close to even but high enough that the organization treated it as a retention risk and denied the promotion. This is not a certainty that you will resign; it is a risk estimate that influenced the decision.

The strongest factor was your overall work experience. Your 1–5 years is common among employees predicted to stay—about half have that range—so this factor worked in your favor. The second factor was whether you have other job opportunities. You reported having them; only about 23% of employees predicted to stay did, so this was the clearest signal pushing toward leaving. The third factor was your medical sector. It is fairly common among stayers—about 31%—and modestly reduced the leave risk. So the top three signals are mixed: experience and sector favored staying, while outside opportunities favored leaving. Taken together, those signals still leave you at a borderline retention risk.

Before a future promotion is reconsidered, discuss your career path and how the organization can improve recognition, pay-for-effort satisfaction, useful training, emotional commitment, job stability and support. If other opportunities are real, the priority should be a concrete retention plan, not simply repeating the promotion decision.
